trap: Trap (A): Believes auxin always promotes growth, so expects IAA on the stump to make the buds grow, and thinks a cytokinin cannot work while the apex is intact. | Trap (B): Forgets that cytokinins help overcome apical dominance and assumes an intact apex always keeps the buds dormant. | Trap (C): Misses that S is the vehicle control, assumes lanolin itself suppresses buds, and also ignores the action of cytokinin.
concept: Plant Growth and Development – Apical dominance experiment with auxin and cytokinin

question: A true-breeding angiosperm of genotype rr is used as the female parent and is pollinated with pollen from a true-breeding RR plant. Based on the events of double fertilisation and post-fertilisation development described in NCERT, which option correctly gives the genotypes of (i) the zygote, (ii) the primary endosperm nucleus, (iii) the seed coat and (iv) the pericarp of the resulting fruit, in that order?
explanation: Both male gametes carry R, and the female gametophyte carries r. Syngamy: R + egg (r) gives the zygote Rr. Triple fusion: NCERT says the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, so r + r + R = rrR. Seed coat: NCERT says the integuments of the ovule harden into the protective seed coats. These are maternal sporophytic tissue, so they are rr. Pericarp: the wall of the ovary develops into the wall of the fruit (pericarp), also maternal, so rr. The answer is Rr ; rrR ; rr ; rr (B).
trap: Trap (A): Reverses the parental contribution to the endosperm (two paternal sets, one maternal) and assumes the seed coat comes from the zygote. | Trap (C): Assumes the seed coat and pericarp develop from products of fertilisation and so carry the hybrid genotype, forgetting that they are maternal tissues. | Trap (D): Treats the endosperm as diploid like the zygote, forgetting that triple fusion involves two polar nuclei.
concept: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants + Principles of Inheritance – Genotypes of zygote, endosperm, seed coat and pericarp

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. The pyramid of energy is always upright, because some energy is lost as heat whenever it flows from one trophic level to the next.
II. In the sea, the pyramid of biomass is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton.
III. Ecological pyramids take saprophytes into account but cannot accommodate a food web.
IV. Of the incident solar radiation, more than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and plants capture 2–10 per cent of this PAR.
V. In an aquatic ecosystem, the detritus food chain is the major conduit for energy flow.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says the pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because some energy is always lost as heat at each step. II – TRUE: NCERT says the pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton. III – FALSE: Among the limitations NCERT lists, ecological pyramids do not accommodate a food web, and saprophytes are given no place in them even though they play a vital role. IV – FALSE: NCERT says less than 50 per cent of incident solar radiation is PAR, and plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR. V – FALSE: NCERT says the grazing food chain is the major conduit in aquatic ecosystems; in terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain. Only I and II are correct, so the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Marks II false, believing every pyramid in every ecosystem must be upright. | Trap (C): Accepts IV after recalling the figure of 50 per cent, but misses that NCERT says PAR is LESS than 50 per cent of incident radiation. | Trap (D): Accepts both III and IV, missing that saprophytes get no place in pyramids and that PAR is under 50 per cent.
concept: Ecosystem – Energy flow, productivity and ecological pyramids

question:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I:
a. Introduction of Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture
b. Extinction of Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon
c. Loss of the parasite species unique to a host fish when the host becomes extinct
d. Wildlife safari parks
e. Biodiversity hotspots
List-II:
i. Alien species invasion
ii. Over-exploitation
iii. Co-extinction
iv. In situ conservation
v. Ex situ conservation
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: a-i: NCERT says the illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens the indigenous catfishes in our rivers. This is an alien species invasion. b-ii: NCERT attributes many extinctions of the last 500 years, such as Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon, to over-exploitation by humans. c-iii: NCERT says that when a host fish becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites meets the same fate. This is co-extinction. d-v: NCERT lists zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks under ex situ conservation, where threatened species are taken out of their natural habitat. e-iv: Biodiversity hotspots, like biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries, are in situ approaches that protect whole ecosystems. So the answer is D.
trap: Trap (A): Thinks safari parks are in situ because the animals roam large natural-looking areas, and puts hotspots under ex situ. | Trap (B): Reads 'aquaculture' as harvesting fish (over-exploitation) and blames the sea cow's extinction on an invader. | Trap (C): Mixes up co-extinction with over-exploitation, missing that the sea cow and passenger pigeon were lost to human over-harvesting.
concept: Biodiversity and Conservation – Causes of biodiversity loss and in situ vs ex situ conservation
review_note: Faculty flag: Mild PYQ overlap: Clarias and Steller's sea cow rows are NEET 2019 Odisha single-item facts.

question: Genes M and N lie on the same chromosome, 20 map units apart. Take recombination frequency as equal to map distance, as in Sturtevant's method, and ignore double crossovers. A true-breeding MMnn plant is crossed with a true-breeding mmNN plant. The F1 is test-crossed with mmnn, and 1000 progeny are raised. What are the expected numbers of progeny that are (dominant for both traits ; recessive for both traits)?
explanation: The parents MMnn and mmNN each give one dominant and one recessive linked allele, so the F1 is Mn/mN (repulsion). NCERT (Morgan) says linked genes give many more parental than recombinant combinations, and Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of the distance between genes. With 20% recombination, the F1 gametes are Mn 40%, mN 40% (parental), MN 10% and mn 10% (recombinant). In a test cross the phenotype shows the F1 gamete. MN gives M_N_ (dominant for both) = 10% of 1000 = 100. mn gives mmnn (recessive for both) = 100. The parental classes Mmnn and mmNn have 400 each. So the answer is 100 ; 100 (A).
trap: Trap (B): Assumes the F1 is in coupling (MN/mn) and treats MN and mn as parental classes, ignoring how the parental cross was set up. | Trap (C): Applies Mendel's independent assortment (1:1:1:1), ignoring that the genes are linked. | Trap (D): Takes the total recombination frequency (20%) as the frequency of each recombinant class instead of splitting it between the two.
concept: Principles of Inheritance and Variation – Linkage, recombination and test cross in repulsion phase

question: An E. coli culture grown for many generations in 14NH4Cl (all DNA light) is transferred to a medium whose only nitrogen source is 15NH4Cl. DNA is extracted at intervals and separated by CsCl density-gradient centrifugation. Assume a generation time of 20 minutes, as stated in NCERT, and semiconservative replication. What is the expected ratio of hybrid (15N/14N) : heavy (15N/15N) : light (14N/14N) DNA at 60 minutes?
explanation: Under semiconservative replication each new duplex keeps one parental strand. Generation 1 (20 min): 2 hybrid molecules. Generation 2 (40 min): 2 hybrid + 2 heavy. Generation 3 (60 min): 8 molecules, of which only the 2 that carry an original light strand are hybrid, and the other 6 are heavy. No light-light molecule can form because the two light strands never pair again. Hybrid : heavy : light = 2 : 6 : 0 = 1 : 3 : 0. This mirrors the NCERT experiment, in which E. coli moved from 15N to 14N gave hybrid DNA after 20 minutes and equal hybrid and light DNA after 40 minutes. A conservative model would instead give 0 : 7 : 1. So the answer is C.
trap: Trap (A): Memorises the original Meselson–Stahl result (hybrid plus light) and does not notice that the labels are reversed here. | Trap (B): Counts only two generations (40 minutes), when 60 minutes is three. | Trap (D): Applies the conservative model, in which the parental light duplex stays intact and every new molecule is fully heavy.
concept: Molecular Basis of Inheritance – Meselson–Stahl experiment (reverse-labelling reasoning)

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. AUG has dual functions: it codes for methionine and also acts as the initiator codon.
II. Each of the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA is read by a specific tRNA that carries no amino acid, and this terminates translation.
III. In the first phase of translation, amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA, a process called charging of tRNA.
IV. In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as the enzyme (ribozyme) for peptide-bond formation.
V. Untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNA are present only at the 5′-end, before the start codon, and are required for efficient translation.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says AUG has dual functions, coding for methionine and acting as the initiator codon. II – FALSE: No tRNA reads the stop codons. NCERT says a release factor binds to the stop codon, ending translation and releasing the polypeptide. III – TRUE: NCERT calls the ATP-dependent activation of amino acids and their linking to cognate tRNA 'charging of tRNA' (aminoacylation). IV – TRUE: NCERT says that in bacteria 23S rRNA is the enzyme, a ribozyme, for peptide-bond formation. V – FALSE: NCERT says UTRs are present at both the 5′-end (before the start codon) and the 3′-end (after the stop codon), and are needed for efficient translation. Three statements (I, III, IV) are correct, so the answer is C.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects both III and IV, confusing aminoacylation with initiation and believing that peptide bonds are made by a ribosomal protein. | Trap (B): Rejects IV, assuming the catalyst must be a protein, although NCERT calls bacterial 23S rRNA a ribozyme. | Trap (D): Accepts II or V, imagining a 'stop tRNA' (termination actually uses a release factor) or remembering UTRs only at the 5′-end.
concept: Molecular Basis of Inheritance – Genetic code and mechanism of translation

question:
Match List-I (family) with List-II (feature shown by its NCERT example plant).
List-I:
a. Malvaceae
b. Cruciferae
c. Leguminosae
d. Compositae
e. Gramineae
List-II:
i. Basal placentation – a single ovule attached at the base of the ovary
ii. Parietal placentation – ovary one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to a false septum
iii. Marginal placentation, with diadelphous stamens and vexillary aestivation
iv. Axile placentation, with stamens united into one bunch
v. Seed with one large shield-shaped cotyledon, a bulky endosperm and a plumule enclosed in a sheath
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: a-iv: China rose (Malvaceae) is NCERT's example of axile placentation and of monoadelphous stamens (united into one bunch). b-ii: Mustard (Cruciferae) is NCERT's example of parietal placentation, where the one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered because of a false septum. c-iii: Pea (Leguminosae/Fabaceae) has marginal placentation, diadelphous stamens and vexillary aestivation (the NCERT Fabaceae description). d-i: Sunflower and marigold (Compositae) are NCERT's examples of basal placentation, with a single ovule at the base. e-v: The NCERT maize grain (Gramineae) has a large shield-shaped cotyledon (scutellum), a bulky endosperm and a plumule enclosed in a coleoptile. So the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Sees mustard's two-chambered ovary and calls it axile, then gives parietal placentation to the Malvaceae. | Trap (C): Confuses basal placentation (sunflower) with parietal (mustard), since in both the ovules seem to sit on the ovary wall or base. | Trap (D): Swaps the 'adelphous' conditions, giving monoadelphous stamens to pea and diadelphous stamens to china rose.
concept: Morphology of Flowering Plants – Diagnostic floral and seed features of syllabus families

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. In bryophytes, the main plant body is the haploid gametophyte, and the sporophyte is not free-living but is attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte, from which it derives nourishment.
II. In pteridophytes, the gametophyte (prothallus) is multicellular and free-living, and it is the dominant phase of the life cycle.
III. Selaginella and Salvinia are homosporous, yet their female gametophytes are retained on the parent sporophyte, a precursor to the seed habit.
IV. In gymnosperms, the male and female gametophytes have an independent, free-living existence outside the sporangia.
V. In mosses, the protonema, the first stage of the gametophyte, develops directly from the zygote.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says the bryophyte plant body is a haploid gametophyte, and the sporophyte is attached to it and derives nourishment from it. II – FALSE: In pteridophytes the main plant body is the sporophyte. The prothallus is small, multicellular, free-living and mostly photosynthetic, but it is not dominant. III – FALSE: NCERT says Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, producing macro- and microspores. Keeping the female gametophyte on the sporophyte is a precursor to the seed habit. IV – FALSE: NCERT says gymnosperm gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence; they stay within the sporangia retained on the sporophyte. V – FALSE: In mosses the protonema develops directly from a spore. Only statement I is correct, so the answer is A.
trap: Trap (B): Accepts III, forgetting that Selaginella and Salvinia are NCERT's examples of heterospory. | Trap (C): Accepts III and V, missing heterospory and thinking the protonema comes from the zygote rather than from a spore. | Trap (D): Muddles which generation dominates and accepts II, III and IV together.
concept: Plant Kingdom – Dominant generation and gametophyte features in bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. In the Krebs cycle, the conversion of succinyl CoA to succinic acid is coupled with the synthesis of a GTP, which in a coupled reaction is converted to GDP while ATP is synthesised from ADP.
II. Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA by pyruvic dehydrogenase takes place in the cytoplasm, after which acetyl CoA enters the mitochondrial matrix.
III. In complex V, the F1 headpiece is the site of ATP synthesis, and for each ATP produced 2H+ pass through F0 from the intermembrane space to the matrix.
IV. The respiratory quotient of tripalmitin is about 0.7, while that of proteins is about 0.9.
V. In alcoholic fermentation, yeasts poison themselves to death when the alcohol concentration reaches about 13 per cent.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says that when succinyl CoA is oxidised to succinic acid a GTP is synthesised (substrate-level phosphorylation), and in a coupled reaction GTP is converted to GDP while ATP is formed from ADP. II – FALSE: NCERT says pyruvate first enters the mitochondrial matrix, where pyruvic dehydrogenase carries out its oxidative decarboxylation; this does not happen in the cytoplasm. III – TRUE: NCERT says F1 is the headpiece containing the site for ATP synthesis, F0 forms the proton channel, and 2H+ pass through it for each ATP. IV – TRUE: NCERT gives tripalmitin RQ = 0.7 and protein RQ of about 0.9. V – TRUE: NCERT says yeasts poison themselves to death at about 13 per cent alcohol. Four statements are correct, so the answer is D.
trap: Trap (A): Treats every numerical detail (2H+, 0.7/0.9, 13%) as altered and accepts only I. | Trap (B): Rejects III and IV, swapping the roles of F0 and F1 and misremembering the RQ of protein. | Trap (C): Rejects V or III, recalling a different alcohol-tolerance limit or the proton count, although both match NCERT.
concept: Respiration in Plants – Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, RQ and fermentation

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. Less than 2 per cent of the human genome codes for proteins, and functions are known for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes.
II. On density-gradient centrifugation, the bulk genomic DNA forms the minor peaks while satellite DNA forms the major peak.
III. About 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences (SNPs) occur in humans have been identified.
IV. VNTR belongs to the mini-satellite class of satellite DNA, and its size varies from 0.1 to 20 kb.
V. Satellite DNA sequences normally do not code for any proteins, and they form only a small portion of the human genome.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – FALSE: NCERT says less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins, but the functions are UNKNOWN for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes. II – FALSE: NCERT says the bulk DNA forms the major peak, and the other small peaks are called satellite DNA. III – TRUE: NCERT reports about 1.4 million SNP locations in humans. IV – TRUE: NCERT says VNTR belongs to the class of satellite DNA called mini-satellite, and its size varies from 0.1 to 20 kb. V – FALSE: NCERT says these sequences normally do not code for any proteins, but they form a large portion of the human genome. Only III and IV are correct, so the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects IV, placing VNTRs among the micro-satellites or misremembering the 0.1–20 kb range. | Trap (C): Accepts V because its first half (non-coding) is correct, missing that NCERT says satellite DNA forms a LARGE portion of the genome. | Trap (D): Accepts I and II, trusting the correct '<2% coding' half of I and swapping the major and minor peaks in II.
concept: Molecular Basis of Inheritance – Human Genome Project findings and DNA fingerprinting
review_note: Faculty flag: Human Genome tagged Zoology; house convention elsewhere is Botany.

question:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I:
a. Interferons secreted by virus-infected cells
b. Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes
c. Mucus coating the epithelium of the respiratory tract
d. PMNL-neutrophils and natural killer cells
e. IgA-rich colostrum received by the newborn
List-II:
i. Physical barrier
ii. Physiological barrier
iii. Cellular barrier
iv. Cytokine barrier
v. Passive immunity
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: NCERT's four innate barriers: a-iv: Interferons are proteins secreted by virus-infected cells that protect non-infected cells, so they are the cytokine barrier. b-ii: Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes prevent microbial growth, so they are physiological barriers. c-i: NCERT groups skin and the mucus coating the epithelium of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts, which traps microbes, as physical barriers. d-iii: PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, NK cells and macrophages phagocytose and destroy microbes, so they are cellular barriers. e-v: NCERT says the IgA-rich colostrum protects the infant and is an example of passive immunity, because ready-made antibodies are received. So the answer is C.
trap: Trap (A): Calls secretions such as acid, saliva and tears 'physical' and calls mucus 'physiological', reversing NCERT's grouping. | Trap (B): Thinks interferons are a cellular defence and leukocytes a cytokine barrier, confusing a secreted protein with the cell that makes it. | Trap (D): Makes both swaps at once, misplacing both the secretions and the interferons and leukocytes.
concept: Human Health and Disease – Barriers of innate immunity and passive immunity
review_note: Faculty flag: PYQ closeness: same four barrier pairings as NEET 2022 Ph-2 / Re-NEET 2022 (original kept by owner's choice).

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. Heroin, chemically diacetylmorphine, is obtained by acetylation of morphine extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum; it is a depressant and slows down body functions.
II. Cocaine, obtained from the coca plant Erythroxylum coca, native to South America, interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine.
III. Cannabinoids interact with opioid receptors present in the central nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract.
IV. Nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and noradrenaline, and smoking increases the oxyhaemoglobin concentration of blood.
V. MRI uses strong magnetic fields and ionising radiations to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says heroin (smack) is diacetylmorphine, obtained by acetylation of morphine from the latex of Papaver somniferum, and is a depressant that slows down body functions. II – TRUE: NCERT says cocaine, from Erythroxylum coca (native to South America), interferes with the transport of dopamine. III – FALSE: Opioids bind specific opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract. Cannabinoids interact with cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. IV – FALSE: Nicotine does stimulate the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, but NCERT says smoking increases the carbon monoxide content of blood and reduces the concentration of haem-bound oxygen. V – FALSE: NCERT says MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations. Only I and II are correct, so the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects II, attributing cocaine's action to a different neurotransmitter, such as serotonin, instead of dopamine. | Trap (C): Accepts III, mixing up cannabinoid receptors in the brain with the opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract. | Trap (D): Accepts IV and V, missing that smoking raises carbon monoxide and lowers oxyhaemoglobin, and that MRI uses non-ionising radiation.
concept: Human Health and Disease – Drugs, tobacco and cancer detection

question: In an isolated myofibril, a resting sarcomere measures 2.6 µm. Its A band is 1.6 µm and its H zone is 0.6 µm. During a contraction the sarcomere shortens to 2.2 µm. Assuming the sliding filament theory as described in NCERT, which option gives the expected (A-band length ; total I-band length within the sarcomere ; H-zone width) after contraction?
explanation: NCERT says that during contraction the thin (actin) filaments slide over the thick (myosin) filaments towards the centre of the A band. The Z lines are pulled inwards, the sarcomere shortens, the I bands get reduced and the A band keeps its length. At rest, total I = 2.6 − 1.6 = 1.0 µm. The shortening of 0.4 µm comes out of the I band: 1.0 − 0.4 = 0.6 µm, and the A band stays at 1.6 µm. The H zone is the central part of the thick filaments not overlapped by thin filaments. The thin filaments from both sides each move 0.2 µm inward, so the H zone narrows by 0.4 µm: 0.6 − 0.4 = 0.2 µm. Check: 1.6 + 0.6 = 2.2 µm. So the answer is D.
trap: Trap (A): Believes the thick filaments themselves shorten, so the A band shrinks while the I band stays the same. | Trap (B): Assumes the H zone cannot change because it lies inside the A band, whose length is constant. | Trap (C): Lets only one set of thin filaments slide into the H zone, so the H zone shrinks by half the actual amount.
concept: Locomotion and Movement – Sliding filament theory: band changes during contraction

question:
In an adult male laboratory mammal, only the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is surgically removed; the hypothalamus, posterior pituitary and all other glands remain intact. Which of the following hormones would show a marked fall in blood level?
(i) Thyroxine
(ii) Cortisol
(iii) Testosterone
(iv) Insulin
(v) Aldosterone
(vi) Oxytocin
explanation: The hypothalamus controls target glands through the anterior pituitary, and target hormones normally feed back on this axis. Removing the adenohypophysis breaks the middle link, so target glands that depend on its trophic hormones fail. (i) TSH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones, so thyroxine falls. (ii) NCERT says ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoids, so cortisol falls. (iii) LH (ICSH) stimulates androgen synthesis in the testis, so testosterone falls. (iv) Insulin from the β-cells of the pancreas responds to blood glucose and does not need the pituitary. (v) Aldosterone is mainly controlled by RAAS (Excretory chapter): angiotensin II activates the adrenal cortex to release it, so it does not fall markedly. (vi) Oxytocin is synthesised by the hypothalamus and released from the intact neurohypophysis. So only (i), (ii) and (iii) fall, which is option A.
trap: Trap (B): Assumes ACTH controls every adrenal cortical hormone and forgets that aldosterone is mainly regulated by the renin–angiotensin system. | Trap (C): Thinks oxytocin comes from the anterior pituitary, although it is made by the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis. | Trap (D): Swaps the targets of ACTH, linking it to mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) instead of glucocorticoids (cortisol).
concept: Chemical Coordination + Excretory Products – Hypothalamus–pituitary–target gland axis vs RAAS control

question: A person loses a large volume of blood in an accident, and blood pressure and body-fluid volume fall. Within the next hour, which option correctly predicts the (renin release from JG cells ; ADH release from the neurohypophysis ; tonicity of the filtrate entering the DCT relative to plasma ; tonicity of the final urine relative to plasma)?
explanation: Renin: NCERT says a fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates the JG cells to release renin. Renin leads to angiotensin II, which raises blood pressure, and to aldosterone, which increases Na+ and water reabsorption. So renin increases. ADH: NCERT says osmoreceptors are activated by changes in blood volume, body-fluid volume and ionic concentration, and excessive fluid loss makes the hypothalamus release ADH from the neurohypophysis. So ADH increases. Filtrate entering the DCT: the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes, so the filtrate gets diluted as it moves up and arrives hypotonic whatever the hormonal state. Final urine: ADH-driven water reabsorption in the collecting duct against the medullary gradient (up to about 1200 mOsmol/L) gives concentrated, hypertonic urine. So the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Thinks ADH responds only to a rise in blood osmolarity, forgetting that NCERT names loss of blood or fluid volume as a stimulus. | Trap (C): Assumes the filtrate is already concentrated as it leaves the loop of Henle because the medulla is hypertonic, ignoring that the ascending limb is impermeable to water. | Trap (D): Thinks low pressure suppresses the JG cells, which reverses the actual JGA response.
concept: Excretory Products and their Elimination – RAAS, ADH and counter-current concentration after haemorrhage

question:
Match List-I (animal) with List-II (feature).
List-I:
a. Pleurobrachia
b. Physalia
c. Balanoglossus
d. Branchiostoma
e. Ascidia
List-II:
i. Notochord present only in the larval tail
ii. Notochord extends from head to tail and persists throughout life
iii. Rudimentary stomochord in the collar region; excretion by a proboscis gland
iv. Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates; bioluminescence
v. Stinging cells used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: a-iv: Pleurobrachia is a ctenophore (comb jelly). NCERT says its body bears eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, and bioluminescence is well marked. b-v: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war) is a cnidarian. Its cnidoblasts are used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey. c-iii: Balanoglossus is a hemichordate. NCERT says it has a rudimentary stomochord, similar to a notochord, in the collar region, and its excretory organ is the proboscis gland. d-ii: Branchiostoma is a cephalochordate, in which the notochord extends from head to tail and persists throughout life. e-i: Ascidia is a urochordate, in which the notochord is present only in the larval tail. So the answer is C.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps the urochordate and cephalochordate notochord patterns (Ascidia vs Branchiostoma). | Trap (B): Treats both jelly-like marine animals as interchangeable and gives the comb plates to Physalia and the cnidoblasts to Pleurobrachia. | Trap (D): Treats the hemichordate stomochord as a true persistent notochord and pushes Branchiostoma's feature onto Balanoglossus.
concept: Animal Kingdom – Diagnostic features of Ctenophora, Cnidaria, Hemichordata and protochordates
review_note: Faculty flag: Mild PYQ overlap: Pleurobrachia and stomochord rows also in the NEET 2024 match.

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. In pBR322, the rop gene codes for the proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid.
II. Ligation of foreign DNA at the BamHI site of pBR322 inactivates the ampicillin-resistance gene, so recombinants grow on tetracycline but not on ampicillin.
III. In the β-galactosidase insertional-inactivation system, recombinant colonies produce blue colour in the presence of a chromogenic substrate.
IV. During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move towards the cathode, and larger fragments move farther.
V. Bacterial cells are made competent by treating them with a specific concentration of a monovalent cation such as sodium, followed by a heat shock at 42 °C.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says rop codes for the proteins involved in plasmid replication. II – FALSE: NCERT says ligation at the BamHI site of the tetracycline-resistance gene inactivates tetR. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline. III – FALSE: An insert in the β-galactosidase coding region stops colour formation, so recombinant colonies stay colourless and non-recombinants turn blue. IV – FALSE: DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode, and the smaller fragments move farther. V – FALSE: NCERT uses a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, then incubation on ice, a heat shock at 42 °C and a return to ice. Only statement I is correct, so the answer is A.
trap: Trap (B): Accepts II, forgetting that NCERT places the BamHI site inside the tetracycline-resistance gene. | Trap (C): Accepts II and V, misplacing BamHI and remembering 'a cation' without noting that it must be divalent (Ca2+). | Trap (D): Gets the logic of insertional inactivation and electrophoresis backwards, accepting blue recombinant colonies, movement towards the cathode and BamHI in ampR.
concept: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes – pBR322, insertional inactivation, electrophoresis and competence

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. Bt toxin exists as an inactive protoxin; inside the insect it becomes active because the alkaline pH of the gut solubilises the crystals.
II. The proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control the corn borer, whereas the protein encoded by cryIAb controls cotton bollworms.
III. To protect tobacco against Meloidogyne incognita, nematode-specific genes were introduced through Agrobacterium vectors; the host produced both sense and anti-sense RNA, which formed dsRNA, initiated RNAi and silenced the nematode's specific mRNA.
IV. In the first clinical gene therapy (1990), for ADA deficiency, a functional ADA cDNA was introduced into the patient's lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, and this gave a permanent cure.
V. In 1983, Eli Lilly produced human insulin by introducing a single DNA sequence encoding proinsulin, including its C-peptide, into a plasmid of E. coli.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says Bt toxin is an inactive protoxin that becomes active in the alkaline pH of the insect gut, which solubilises the crystals. The toxin binds midgut epithelial cells, forms pores, and the cells swell and lyse. II – FALSE: NCERT says cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, and cryIAb controls the corn borer. III – TRUE: NCERT describes exactly this RNAi strategy against Meloidogyne incognita. IV – FALSE: Lymphocytes are not immortal, so NCERT says the patient needs periodic infusions; a permanent cure would need the gene introduced into cells at early embryonic stages. V – FALSE: NCERT says Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains, put them into E. coli plasmids, and combined the chains by disulphide bonds. Only I and III are correct, so the answer is B.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects III, not realising that the host itself made both the sense and the anti-sense RNA. | Trap (C): Accepts V, not recalling that Eli Lilly prepared two separate DNA sequences, for chains A and B. | Trap (D): Accepts II and IV, swapping the cry genes for cotton and corn and assuming the 1990 therapy was permanent.
concept: Biotechnology and its Applications – Bt crops, RNAi, gene therapy and recombinant insulin

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. In the tissues, high pCO2, high H+ concentration and higher temperature favour the dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.
II. Under normal physiological conditions, every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O2 to the tissues, and every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO2 to the alveoli.
III. The pO2 of deoxygenated blood equals that of the tissues (40 mm Hg), whereas its pCO2 (45 mm Hg) exceeds that of alveolar air (40 mm Hg).
IV. About 20–25 per cent of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate, while about 70 per cent is carried by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin.
V. The chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to O2 and H+, whereas the role of CO2 in regulating the respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says low pO2, high pCO2, high H+ and higher temperature in the tissues favour the dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin. II – TRUE: These are NCERT's figures, about 5 mL O2 and 4 mL CO2 per 100 mL of blood. III – TRUE: NCERT's table gives deoxygenated blood pO2 40 and pCO2 45, tissues 40 and 45, and alveoli 104 and 40 mm Hg. IV – FALSE: NCERT says 20–25 per cent of CO2 is carried by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin and about 70 per cent as bicarbonate. V – FALSE: NCERT says the chemosensitive area is highly sensitive to CO2 and H+, and that the role of OXYGEN in regulating the respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant. Statements I, II and III are correct, so the answer is C.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects II and III, misremembering the 5 mL / 4 mL delivery figures and the 40/45 mm Hg values in NCERT's table. | Trap (B): Rejects III, assuming deoxygenated blood must have a lower pO2 than the tissues it has just left. | Trap (D): Accepts IV, swapping the bicarbonate (about 70%) and carbamino-haemoglobin (20–25%) fractions.
concept: Breathing and Exchange of Gases – Partial pressures, gas transport and regulation of respiration

question:
Match List-I (developmental event in the human embryo or foetus) with List-II (time of pregnancy).
List-I:
a. Formation of the heart
b. Development of limbs and digits
c. Formation of most major organ systems, with limbs and external genital organs well developed
d. First movements of the foetus and appearance of hair on the head
e. Body covered with fine hair, eyelids separate and eyelashes formed
List-II:
i. During the fifth month
ii. After one month
iii. By the end of the second trimester (about 24 weeks)
iv. By the end of the second month
v. By the end of the first trimester (12 weeks)
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: NCERT sequence: a-ii: after one month of pregnancy, the embryo's heart is formed. b-iv: by the end of the second month, the foetus develops limbs and digits. c-v: by the end of 12 weeks (first trimester), most of the major organ systems are formed, and the limbs and external genital organs are well developed. d-i: the first movements of the foetus and the appearance of hair on the head are usually observed during the fifth month. e-iii: by the end of about 24 weeks (second trimester), the body is covered with fine hair, the eyelids separate and the eyelashes are formed. So the answer is D.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps the end of the first trimester and the end of the second trimester, placing organ-system formation at 24 weeks. | Trap (B): Reverses the first two milestones, thinking limbs and digits appear before the heart. | Trap (C): Confuses hair on the head (fifth month) with fine hair covering the body (end of 24 weeks).
concept: Human Reproduction – Timeline of embryonic and foetal development
review_note: Faculty flag: PYQ closeness: same embryo-timeline pairings as NEET 2024 (original kept by owner's choice).

question:
Consider the following statements:
I. The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are homologous organs and represent divergent evolution.
II. Sweet potato and potato are analogous organs; the former is a stem modification and the latter a root modification.
III. In S.L. Miller's experiment, an electric discharge was passed through CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 °C in a closed flask, and amino acids were formed.
IV. Homo habilis had a brain capacity of 650–800 cc and probably did not eat meat, whereas Homo erectus had a brain of about 900 cc and probably ate meat.
V. Neanderthal man, with a brain size of 1400 cc, lived in near-east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years back and buried their dead.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explanation: I – TRUE: NCERT says the thorns and tendrils of Bougainvillea and Cucurbita represent homology, which comes from divergent evolution. II – FALSE: NCERT gives sweet potato (a root modification) and potato (a stem modification) as analogous organs, so the statement swaps them. III – TRUE: NCERT says Miller (1953) created an electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 °C and observed amino acids forming. IV – TRUE: NCERT gives H. habilis 650–800 cc and probably no meat, and H. erectus about 900 cc and probably ate meat. V – TRUE: NCERT says Neanderthal man, with a brain of 1400 cc, lived in near-east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years back, used hides and buried their dead. Four statements are correct, so the answer is D.
trap: Trap (A): Treats every numerical detail (800 °C, 650–800 cc, 900 cc, 1400 cc) as altered and rejects III, IV and V. | Trap (B): Doubts the 800 °C figure and swaps the meat-eating habit between H. habilis and H. erectus, rejecting III and IV. | Trap (C): Rejects III, thinking 800 °C is implausibly high for a prebiotic simulation, although it is NCERT's own figure.
concept: Evolution – Homology/analogy, Miller's experiment and human evolution

question:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I:
a. P-wave of a standard ECG
b. The point shortly after Q of the QRS complex
c. T-wave
d. First heart sound (lub)
e. Second heart sound (dub)
List-II:
i. Closure of the semilunar valves
ii. Return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state
iii. Beginning of ventricular systole
iv. Closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves
v. Depolarisation of the atria leading to their contraction
Choose the correct answer.
explanation: a-v: NCERT says the P-wave represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to contraction of both atria. b-iii: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation, and NCERT says contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole. c-ii: The T-wave represents the return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation); the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole. d-iv: The first heart sound (lub) comes from the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves. e-i: The second heart sound (dub) comes from the closure of the semilunar valves. So the answer is A.
trap: Trap (B): Swaps the heart sounds, linking lub to the semilunar valves and dub to the atrioventricular valves. | Trap (C): Thinks the P-wave marks the start of systole and links the QRS region to atrial depolarisation. | Trap (D): Mixes up depolarisation and repolarisation, thinking the T-wave starts systole and the Q region shows ventricular recovery.
concept: Body Fluids and Circulation – ECG waves and heart sounds in the cardiac cycle
review_note: Faculty flag: PYQ closeness: NEET 2023 Ph-1 ECG match pairings (original kept by owner's choice).

question: Which hormone secreted by the pineal gland plays an important role in regulating the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body?
explanation: NCERT: the pineal gland lies on the dorsal side of the forebrain and secretes melatonin, which plays a very important role in regulating the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body, such as the sleep-wake cycle and body temperature. Melatonin also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and defence capability. MSH comes from the pars intermedia, vasopressin from the hypothalamus (stored and released by the posterior pituitary), and TCT from the thyroid.
trap: Trap (A): Links 'pigmentation' (an effect of melatonin) to MSH and forgets that MSH comes from the pars intermedia of the pituitary | Trap (B): Assumes every hormone near the brain's midline is pineal; vasopressin is made by the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis | Trap (D): Mixes up two small endocrine glands; thyrocalcitonin comes from the thyroid and regulates blood calcium
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – Pineal gland and melatonin

question: The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce a peptide hormone that stimulates the formation of RBCs. This hormone is:
explanation: NCERT (hormones of heart, kidney and GI tract): the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce a peptide hormone called erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (formation of RBCs). Renin, also released by JG cells, converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I in blood pressure and GFR regulation. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex.
trap: Trap (A): Remembers that JG cells release renin but forgets that renin acts in the renin–angiotensin pathway and not on erythropoiesis | Trap (C): Treats angiotensin II, a product of the JGA pathway, as a JG cell hormone with a blood-forming role | Trap (D): Links the kidney with aldosterone, which is an adrenal cortex hormone acting on the renal tubules
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – Hormones of kidney (erythropoietin)

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) Glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes and is a hyperglycemic hormone.
(ii) Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes and stimulates glycogenesis.
(iii) The adrenal medulla secretes aldosterone in response to stress.
(iv) Cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses the immune response.
(v) Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis.
explanation: (i) True – glucagon acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes), stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and raises blood glucose. (ii) True – insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes, enhances glucose uptake and utilisation, and stimulates glycogenesis. (iii) False – aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex; the medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline (the 'emergency hormones'). (iv) True – NCERT states that cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses the immune response. (v) True – glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis. Four statements are correct.
trap: Trap (A): Accepts only the glucagon statement, thinking insulin acts only on muscle and that cortisol is pro-inflammatory | Trap (B): Rejects (iv) and (v), believing glucocorticoids only raise blood glucose and have no immune or lipid/protein effects | Trap (C): Accepts gluconeogenesis but rejects lipolysis and proteolysis in (v), forgetting that NCERT lists all three together
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – Pancreatic and adrenal hormones

question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): FSH normally does not enter its target cells but brings about its effects through second messengers such as cyclic AMP.
Reason (R): Being a protein hormone of the pituitary, FSH binds to membrane-bound receptors on the target cell.
Choose the correct answer.
option_A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_C: A is true but R is false
option_D: A is false but R is true
explanation: NCERT classifies pituitary hormones as peptide/protein hormones. NCERT's mechanism of protein hormone action shows that such hormones bind to membrane-bound receptors. Hormones that interact with membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the target cell. Instead, they generate second messengers (cyclic AMP, IP3, Ca++), which regulate cellular metabolism. FSH acts this way because it binds a membrane receptor, so R correctly explains A. By contrast, steroid hormones and iodothyronines bind intracellular receptors and regulate gene expression.
trap: Trap (B): Sees both facts as true but does not link the type of receptor (membrane-bound) to the second-messenger route | Trap (C): Thinks FSH is a steroid because it acts on the gonads, which make steroid hormones | Trap (D): Believes all hormones enter the cell and act on genes, ignoring the second-messenger mechanism
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – Mechanism of hormone action

question:
Match List I (hormone) with List II (action):
List I: (a) Gastrin (b) Secretin (c) Cholecystokinin (d) Gastric inhibitory peptide (e) Thyrocalcitonin
List II: (i) Inhibits gastric secretion and motility (ii) Stimulates secretion of water and bicarbonate ions from the exocrine pancreas (iii) Regulates blood calcium levels (iv) Stimulates gastric glands to secrete HCl and pepsinogen (v) Stimulates secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice
Choose the correct option.
explanation: a-iv: gastrin acts on gastric glands and stimulates secretion of HCl and pepsinogen. b-ii: secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas and stimulates secretion of water and bicarbonate ions. c-v: CCK acts on both the pancreas and the gall bladder, stimulating secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice. d-i: GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility. e-iii: the thyroid also secretes a protein hormone, thyrocalcitonin (TCT), which regulates blood calcium levels.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps secretin and CCK because both act on the pancreas; forgets that secretin gives water + bicarbonate while CCK gives enzymes + bile | Trap (C): Reverses gastrin and GIP because both have 'gastric' in their role; one stimulates gastric secretion, the other inhibits it | Trap (D): Thinks gastrin stimulates bile and CCK acts on gastric glands, mixing up which organ each hormone targets
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – GI tract hormones and thyrocalcitonin
review_note: Faculty flag: Partial PYQ/coaching overlap: standard GI-hormone match pairings.

question: Which of the following disorders is correctly matched with its hormonal cause?
option_A: Diabetes insipidus – impaired secretion of insulin
option_B: Acromegaly – excess secretion of growth hormone during childhood
option_C: Exophthalmic goitre – hypothyroidism due to iodine deficiency
option_D: Addison's disease – underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex
explanation: NCERT: underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue. This disease is called Addison's disease. Diabetes insipidus results from impaired synthesis or release of ADH, which reduces the kidney's ability to conserve water. Acromegaly is due to excess GH in adults, while excess GH in childhood causes gigantism. Exophthalmic goitre is a form of hyperthyroidism with enlarged thyroid and protruding eyeballs.
trap: Trap (A): Misled by the word 'diabetes'; diabetes insipidus is due to impaired synthesis or release of ADH, not insulin | Trap (B): Confuses gigantism (excess GH in childhood) with acromegaly (excess GH in adults, especially in middle age) | Trap (C): Links every goitre to iodine deficiency; exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism
concept: Chemical Coordination and Integration – Hormonal disorders

question: When a neuron is not conducting any impulse, its axonal membrane is:
option_A: More permeable to Na+ than to K+
option_B: Comparatively more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+
option_C: Equally permeable to Na+ and K+
option_D: Impermeable to both ions, with a pump moving 2 Na+ out for 3 K+ in
explanation: NCERT: at rest, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+. It is also impermeable to the negatively charged proteins in the axoplasm. The ionic gradients are maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, which moves 3 Na+ outwards for 2 K+ into the cell. As a result, the outer surface is positively charged and the inner surface negatively charged (polarised).
trap: Trap (A): Reverses the ions, mixing up the resting state with the Na+ influx that happens on stimulation | Trap (C): Assumes equal permeability, which could not maintain an ionic gradient | Trap (D): Reverses the Na+/K+ pump ratio (actually 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in) and wrongly makes the membrane impermeable to K+
concept: Neural Control and Coordination – Resting membrane permeability

question: Which of the following statements about the human forebrain is correct?
option_A: The cerebral cortex is called white matter because neuron cell bodies with myelin are concentrated there
option_B: The thalamus is a major coordinating centre for sensory signalling only and has no role in motor signalling
option_C: The limbic system lies in the hindbrain and its main role is to control posture and balance
option_D: The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and contains centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking
explanation: NCERT: the hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and contains centres controlling body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking. It also has neurosecretory cells that secrete hypothalamic hormones. The cerebral cortex is grey matter because neuron cell bodies are concentrated there. The thalamus is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. Along with the hypothalamus, the limbic system (inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres) regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions and motivation.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps grey and white matter; the cortex is grey matter (cell bodies), while myelinated tracts form the inner white matter | Trap (B): Remembers 'sensory' but drops 'motor'; NCERT calls the thalamus a coordinating centre for both | Trap (C): Places the limbic system in the wrong brain region; it is formed by the inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres (amygdala, hippocampus) and regulates emotions and sexual behaviour
concept: Neural Control and Coordination – Forebrain parts and functions

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) At electrical synapses, the membranes of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons are in very close proximity.
(ii) Impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than across a chemical synapse.
(iii) At a chemical synapse, the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled space, and neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
(iv) Electrical synapses are very common in our nervous system.
(v) Binding of a neurotransmitter always produces an excitatory potential in the post-synaptic neuron.
explanation: (i) True – at electrical synapses the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are very close, and current can flow directly from one neuron to the next. (ii) True – NCERT says transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than across a chemical synapse. (iii) True – at a chemical synapse the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft; neurotransmitters released from vesicles bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane. (iv) False – electrical synapses are rare in our system. (v) False – the new potential can be excitatory or inhibitory. Three statements are correct.
trap: Trap (B): Accepts (iv), assuming the faster type must also be the common type; NCERT says electrical synapses are rare | Trap (C): Rejects (ii), thinking chemical transmission is faster because it involves active release | Trap (D): Accepts only (iii), wrongly treating electrical-synapse features as myths
concept: Neural Control and Coordination – Electrical vs chemical synapse

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) A stimulus makes the membrane at that site freely permeable to Na+, so its outer surface becomes negatively charged.
(ii) The electrical potential difference across the membrane at the stimulated site is called the action potential, also termed a nerve impulse.
(iii) The resting potential at the site of excitation is restored mainly by diffusion of K+ to the outside of the membrane.
(iv) The sodium-potassium pump transports 2 Na+ outwards for every 3 K+ moved into the cell.
(v) At rest, the fluid outside the axon has a low Na+ concentration and a high K+ concentration.
explanation: (i) True – at the stimulated site the membrane becomes freely permeable to Na+; rapid Na+ influx reverses polarity, so the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive. (ii) True – this potential difference is the action potential, termed a nerve impulse. (iii) True – the rise in Na+ permeability is very short-lived and is followed by a rise in K+ permeability; K+ diffuses out and restores the resting potential. (iv) False – the pump moves 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in. (v) False – outside fluid has low K+ and high Na+; the axoplasm has high K+ and low Na+. Three statements are correct.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects (i) and (iii), thinking the outer surface stays positive during excitation and that Na+ outflow causes repolarisation | Trap (B): Rejects (iii), believing the pump (not K+ diffusion) restores the resting potential within a fraction of a second | Trap (D): Misses the reversed numbers in (iv) or the reversed ion distribution in (v)
concept: Neural Control and Coordination – Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): The cerebral cortex is referred to as the grey matter.
Reason (R): The cerebral cortex is made up mainly of myelinated fibre tracts, which give it its colour.
Choose the correct answer.
option_A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_C: A is true but R is false
option_D: A is false but R is true
explanation: NCERT: the layer of cells covering the cerebral hemisphere is the cerebral cortex. It is called grey matter because of its greyish appearance, which comes from the neuron cell bodies concentrated there, so A is true. The myelinated fibres of the tracts form the inner part of the cerebral hemisphere and give it an opaque white appearance (white matter), so R is false.
trap: Trap (A): Thinks myelin gives the grey colour, mixing up the sources of grey and white matter | Trap (B): Accepts both as true facts without checking where the myelinated tracts actually lie | Trap (D): Reverses the terms and calls the cortex white matter
concept: Neural Control and Coordination – Grey and white matter of cerebrum

question: Which leucocytes are the least abundant and secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin?
explanation: NCERT: basophils are the least abundant leucocytes (0.5–1%). They secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin, etc., and are involved in inflammatory reactions. Neutrophils are the most abundant (60–65%), neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic, and eosinophils (2–3%) resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions.
trap: Trap (A): Links allergy with these chemicals; eosinophils resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions but do not secrete histamine and heparin | Trap (B): Confuses 'least' with 'most'; neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs (60–65%) | Trap (C): Picks a large agranulocyte because it is phagocytic, mixing up phagocytes with secretory cells
concept: Body Fluids and Circulation – Types of leucocytes

question: A person with blood group AB can receive blood from donors of all ABO groups because his plasma:
option_A: Lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
option_B: Contains both antigen A and antigen B
option_D: Contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
explanation: NCERT: group AB has antigens A and B on RBCs and no antibodies (neither anti-A nor anti-B) in plasma. Because no antibody in the recipient's plasma can react with donor RBCs, AB persons can accept blood from A, B, AB and O, and are called universal recipients. Group O has both anti-A and anti-B and is the universal donor.
trap: Trap (B): Confuses RBC-surface antigens with plasma antibodies; the antigens are on RBCs, not in plasma, and they do not explain why AB can receive all groups | Trap (C): Brings Rh grouping into an ABO question; the Rh antigen is on RBCs, not in plasma | Trap (D): Describes group O plasma, which carries both antibodies (the universal donor group)
concept: Body Fluids and Circulation – ABO blood grouping

question:
Match List I (component of a standard ECG) with List II (event it represents):
List I: (a) P-wave (b) QRS complex (c) T-wave (d) End of T-wave
List II: (i) Return of ventricles from excited to normal state (ii) End of systole (iii) Depolarisation of atria (iv) Depolarisation of ventricles
Choose the correct option.
explanation: a-iii: the P-wave represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to atrial contraction. b-iv: the QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles, which initiates ventricular contraction. c-i: the T-wave represents the return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation). d-ii: the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps P-wave and QRS, forgetting that atrial depolarisation comes first in the trace | Trap (B): Thinks the T-wave itself marks the end of systole, mixing up the wave with its end point | Trap (D): Swaps QRS and T, mixing up ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation
review_note: Faculty flag: PYQ COPY: identical four pairings to the NEET 2023 Phase 2 ECG match; consider rewriting or rejecting.

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) During joint diastole, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open while the semilunar valves are closed.
(ii) Atrial systole increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent.
(iii) The AVN can generate the maximum number of action potentials, i.e., 70–75 per minute.
(iv) The first heart sound 'lub' is associated with closure of the semilunar valves.
(v) During ventricular systole, the semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds that in the pulmonary artery and aorta.
explanation: (i) True – during joint diastole the AV valves are open and blood flows from the pulmonary veins and vena cava into the ventricles through the atria; the semilunar valves are closed. (ii) True – atrial systole increases flow into the ventricles by about 30%. (iii) False – the SAN generates the maximum number of action potentials (70–75/min) and so acts as the pacemaker. (iv) False – 'lub' is due to closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; 'dub' is due to closure of the semilunar valves. (v) True – rising ventricular pressure opens the semilunar valves and blood flows into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Three statements are correct.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects (i), assuming all valves stay closed when all chambers are relaxed | Trap (C): Falls for (iii), forgetting that the SAN, not the AVN, generates the most action potentials and is the pacemaker | Trap (D): Also accepts (iv), mixing up 'lub' (AV valve closure) with 'dub' (semilunar valve closure)
concept: Body Fluids and Circulation – Cardiac cycle and heart sounds

question: Which of the following disorders of the circulatory system is correctly described?
option_A: Angina pectoris – acute chest pain that appears when not enough oxygen is reaching the heart muscle
option_B: Coronary artery disease – inflammation of the heart valves caused by bacterial infection
option_C: Heart failure – the condition in which the heart stops beating
option_D: Hypertension – repeated blood pressure readings of 120/80 mm Hg or higher
explanation: NCERT: angina pectoris is acute chest pain that appears when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle. It can occur in men and women of any age but is more common among the middle-aged and elderly, and is due to conditions that affect blood flow. CAD (atherosclerosis) narrows the lumen of the arteries supplying the heart muscle. Heart failure is when the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough; it is not the same as cardiac arrest (heart stops beating) or heart attack. Normal BP is 120/80 mm Hg; repeated readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher indicate hypertension.
trap: Trap (B): Does not know that CAD (atherosclerosis) is caused by calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrowing the coronary artery lumen | Trap (C): Mixes up heart failure with cardiac arrest; heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs | Trap (D): Takes the normal value (120/80) as the cut-off; NCERT says repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension
concept: Body Fluids and Circulation – Disorders of circulatory system

question: The axial skeleton of an adult human, made up of the skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs, consists of how many bones?
explanation: NCERT: the human skeleton has 206 bones and a few cartilages, grouped into the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton. The axial skeleton has 80 bones distributed along the main axis of the body: skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The appendicular skeleton (limb bones and girdles) has 126 bones. The vertebral column has 26 vertebrae.
trap: Trap (A): Gives the number of appendicular bones instead of axial bones | Trap (B): Gives the total number of bones in the human skeleton | Trap (C): Gives the number of vertebrae in the vertebral column, which is only one part of the axial skeleton

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) Each actin filament is made of two F-actins helically wound to each other, each F-actin being a polymer of G-actin monomers.
(ii) Two filaments of tropomyosin run close to the F-actins throughout their length.
(iii) The globular head of meromyosin is an active ATPase enzyme with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.
(iv) In the resting state, a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on the actin filaments.
(v) Each myosin filament is a polymer of monomeric units called heavy meromyosin (HMM).
explanation: (i) True – each actin (thin) filament is made of two F (filamentous) actins helically wound; each F-actin is a polymer of G (globular) actin monomers. (ii) True – two tropomyosin filaments run close to the F-actins throughout their length. (iii) True – the globular head is an active ATPase enzyme with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin. (iv) True – troponin is distributed at regular intervals on tropomyosin, and in the resting state a subunit of troponin masks the myosin binding sites on actin. (v) False – myosin is a polymer of monomeric proteins called meromyosins; each meromyosin has a globular head with a short arm (HMM) and a tail (LMM). Four statements are correct.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects (iii) and (iv), thinking the ATPase is on actin and that tropomyosin (not troponin) masks the sites | Trap (B): Rejects (iv), mixing up troponin and tropomyosin as the masking protein | Trap (D): Accepts (v), confusing the monomer (meromyosin) with its HMM component
concept: Locomotion and Movement – Structure of contractile proteins

question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): Visceral (smooth) muscles are involuntary muscles.
Reason (R): Smooth muscle fibres taper at both ends and do not show striations.
Choose the correct answer.
option_A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_C: A is true but R is false
option_D: A is false but R is true
explanation: NCERT: visceral muscles in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs look smooth and are called smooth muscles. Their activities are not under voluntary control of the nervous system, so they are involuntary muscles; A is true. Smooth muscle fibres taper at both ends (fusiform) and do not show striations; R is true. But voluntary or involuntary control depends on nervous control, not on striations. Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary, so R does not explain A.
trap: Trap (A): Assumes that lack of striations makes a muscle involuntary, forgetting that cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary | Trap (C): Thinks smooth muscle fibres are cylindrical and unbranched like skeletal fibres | Trap (D): Mixes up 'smooth' with 'skeletal' and treats visceral muscles as voluntary
concept: Locomotion and Movement – Types of muscles

question:
Match List I (type of joint) with List II (example):
List I: (a) Fibrous joint (b) Cartilaginous joint (c) Pivot joint (d) Saddle joint (e) Gliding joint
List II: (i) Between atlas and axis (ii) Flat skull bones forming the cranium (iii) Between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column (iv) Between the carpals (v) Between carpal and metacarpal of thumb
Choose the correct option.
explanation: a-ii: fibrous joints allow no movement; flat skull bones fuse end-to-end by dense fibrous connective tissue (sutures) to form the cranium. b-iii: in cartilaginous joints bones are joined by cartilage, as between adjacent vertebrae, which permits limited movement. c-i: the pivot joint is between atlas and axis. d-v: the saddle joint is between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb. e-iv: the gliding joint is between the carpals.
trap: Trap (B): Swaps fibrous and cartilaginous joints, forgetting that skull sutures are immovable while vertebral joints allow limited movement | Trap (C): Swaps saddle and gliding joints because both involve carpals | Trap (D): Assumes every joint in the vertebral column is a pivot joint and so places atlas–axis under cartilaginous
concept: Locomotion and Movement – Types of joints
review_note: Faculty flag: PYQ remix: NEET 2019 Odisha joints match (pivot, saddle, gliding rows reused).

question: Which of the following disorders of the muscular and skeletal system is correctly described?
option_A: Myasthenia gravis – progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder
option_B: Tetany – inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals
option_C: Gout – age-related disorder with decreased bone mass, commonly due to decreased levels of estrogen
option_D: Osteoporosis – age-related disorder with decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures
explanation: NCERT: osteoporosis is an age-related disorder with decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased estrogen is a common cause. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, leading to fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle. Muscular dystrophy is progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to genetic disorder. Tetany is rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to low Ca++ in body fluid. Gout is inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals.
trap: Trap (A): Gives the definition of muscular dystrophy; myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction | Trap (B): Gives the definition of gout; tetany is rapid spasms due to low Ca++ in body fluid | Trap (C): Gives the definition of osteoporosis but labels it gout
concept: Locomotion and Movement – Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) The glomerular filtration rate in a healthy individual is approximately 125 mL per minute, i.e., 180 litres per day.
(ii) Nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate has to be reabsorbed by the renal tubules.
(iii) A fall in GFR can activate the JG cells to release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
(iv) ANF causes vasoconstriction and thereby increases blood pressure.
(v) ADH facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule, thereby preventing diuresis.
explanation: (i) True – GFR is about 125 mL/min, i.e., 180 litres per day. (ii) True – since urine released is about 1.5 litres per day, nearly 99% of the filtrate must be reabsorbed. (iii) True – a fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates JG cells to release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then to angiotensin II. (iv) False – ANF causes vasodilation and decreases blood pressure, acting as a check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism. (v) True – ADH facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule and prevents diuresis. Four statements are correct.
trap: Trap (B): Rejects (iii), thinking renin directly forms angiotensin II or is released when GFR rises | Trap (C): Accepts (iv), confusing ANF with angiotensin II, which is the vasoconstrictor; ANF is a vasodilator | Trap (D): Rejects (i) and (ii) because 180 L/day of filtrate seems implausibly large compared with about 1.5 L of urine
concept: Excretory Products and their Elimination – GFR and regulation of kidney function

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) Human kidneys can produce urine nearly four times as concentrated as the initial filtrate formed.
(ii) In cortical nephrons, the loop of Henle is very long and runs deep into the medulla.
(iii) The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium, which increases the surface area for reabsorption.
(iv) Urea plays no role in maintaining the concentration gradient in the medullary interstitium.
(v) The vasa recta is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.
explanation: (i) True – NCERT says human kidneys can produce urine nearly four times as concentrated as the initial filtrate. (ii) False – in the majority of nephrons (cortical) the loop of Henle is too short and extends only very little into the medulla; juxtamedullary nephrons have very long loops that run deep into the medulla. (iii) True – the PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium, which increases the surface area for reabsorption. (iv) False – small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule, which helps maintain the gradient. (v) True – the vasa recta is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons. Three statements are correct.
trap: Trap (A): Rejects (i), wrongly thinking the human kidney cannot concentrate urine beyond the filtrate's own osmolarity | Trap (C): Accepts (ii), reversing cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons, since cortical loops barely enter the medulla | Trap (D): Rejects (iii) and (v) as well, unsure of the PCT epithelium and of how the vasa recta is distributed
concept: Excretory Products and their Elimination – Nephron types and counter-current mechanism

question:
Match List I (excretory structure) with List II (animal):
List I: (a) Protonephridia (flame cells) (b) Nephridia (c) Malpighian tubules (d) Antennal (green) glands
List II: (i) Prawn (ii) Planaria (iii) Earthworm (iv) Most insects
Choose the correct option.
explanation: a-ii: protonephridia (flame cells) are the excretory structures in Platyhelminthes such as Planaria, and are mainly concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation. b-iii: nephridia are the tubular excretory structures of earthworms and other annelids. c-iv: Malpighian tubules are the excretory structures of most insects. d-i: antennal or green glands perform excretion in crustaceans like prawns.
trap: Trap (A): Mixes up the two worm types; flame cells belong to flatworms, nephridia to annelids | Trap (B): Swaps the two arthropods; green glands are crustacean, Malpighian tubules are insect | Trap (C): Gives nephridia to insects and Malpighian tubules to earthworms because both are 'tubular' structures
concept: Excretory Products and their Elimination – Excretory structures in animals
review_note: Faculty flag: Partial: same four pairings as an NCERT Exemplar excretory-structure match.

question: The inner surfaces of hollow organs such as bronchioles and fallopian tubes are lined by:
explanation: NCERT: columnar or cuboidal cells bearing cilia on their free surface are called ciliated epithelium. Their function is to move particles or mucus in a specific direction over the epithelium. They are mainly present on the inner surface of hollow organs like bronchioles and fallopian tubes. Squamous epithelium lines blood vessels and lung air sacs. Compound epithelium covers dry skin, the moist surface of the buccal cavity and the pharynx.
trap: Trap (A): Links the respiratory tract with squamous epithelium, which actually lines blood vessel walls and lung air sacs | Trap (B): Assumes protective multilayered epithelium lines all tubes; compound epithelium covers dry skin, the buccal cavity and the pharynx | Trap (D): Thinks of goblet cells in the airways, but bronchioles and fallopian tubes are lined by ciliated cells that move particles or mucus
concept: Structural Organisation in Animals – Epithelial tissue types

question: Which of the following pairs of cell junction and its function is correct?
option_A: Adhering junctions – perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together
option_B: Tight junctions – connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions
option_C: Gap junctions – stop substances from leaking across a tissue
option_D: Gap junctions – keep neighbouring cells cemented together
explanation: NCERT: three types of junctions occur in epithelial and other tissues. Tight junctions help stop substances from leaking across a tissue. Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together. Gap junctions help cells communicate by connecting the cytoplasm of adjoining cells, allowing rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.
trap: Trap (B): Gives tight junctions the communicating role of gap junctions | Trap (C): Reverses gap and tight junctions; tight junctions are the 'sealing' type | Trap (D): Gives gap junctions the cementing role of adhering junctions
concept: Structural Organisation in Animals – Cell junctions

question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): Tendons attach one bone to another bone.
Reason (R): In dense regular connective tissue, collagen fibres are present in rows between many parallel bundles of fibres.
Choose the correct answer.
option_A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_C: A is true but R is false
option_D: A is false but R is true
explanation: NCERT: in dense regular connective tissue, collagen fibres are present in rows between many parallel bundles of fibres, so R is true. Its examples are tendons, which attach skeletal muscles to bones, and ligaments, which attach one bone to another. A describes a ligament, not a tendon, so A is false. Dense irregular tissue (fibres oriented differently) is present in the skin.
trap: Trap (A): Swaps the roles of tendons and ligaments and then links them to the correct description of tissue structure | Trap (B): Accepts the swapped role of tendons as true and only questions the link between A and R | Trap (C): Mixes up the fibre arrangement of dense regular and dense irregular tissue, so rejects R
concept: Structural Organisation in Animals – Dense regular connective tissue

question: In a human cell dividing in culture with an average cell cycle of 24 hours, the actual cell division (M phase) lasts for:
explanation: NCERT: in a 24-hour average cell cycle of a human cell, cell division proper lasts for only about an hour. The interphase lasts more than 95% of the cycle. During interphase the cell prepares for division by undergoing growth and DNA replication in an orderly manner.
trap: Trap (A): Assumes interphase and M phase share the cycle equally | Trap (B): Guesses a 'quarter of the cycle' without recalling the NCERT figure | Trap (C): Confuses the duration of interphase (more than 95% of the cycle) with that of the M phase
concept: Cell Cycle and Cell Division – Duration of phases

question: Some cells in adult animals do not appear to divide, while others divide only occasionally to replace lost or dead cells. Cells that do not divide further exit the G1 phase and enter an inactive stage called:
explanation: NCERT: cells that do not divide further exit the G1 phase and enter an inactive stage called the quiescent stage (G0) of the cell cycle. Cells in this stage remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so, depending on the organism's requirements. Interkinesis is the short stage between meiosis I and meiosis II.
trap: Trap (A): Thinks cells pause after DNA synthesis, mixing up G2 with the exit from the cycle | Trap (B): Confuses the DNA-synthesis phase with an inactive stage | Trap (D): Brings in the short stage between meiosis I and II, which has nothing to do with leaving the cycle
concept: Cell Cycle and Cell Division – Quiescent stage (G0)

question:
How many of the following statements are correct?
(i) Mitosis usually results in diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement.
(ii) Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division but only a single cycle of DNA replication.
(iii) In plants, mitotic divisions in the apical and lateral cambium result in continuous growth throughout life.
(iv) Meiosis increases genetic variability in the population of organisms from one generation to the next.
(v) In plant cells, cytokinesis takes place by a furrow in the plasma membrane that deepens and joins at the centre.
explanation: (i) True – mitosis usually results in diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement. (ii) True – meiosis has two sequential nuclear and cell divisions (meiosis I and II) but only a single cycle of DNA replication. (iii) True – mitotic divisions in the meristematic tissues (apical and lateral cambium) result in continuous growth of plants throughout their life. (iv) True – meiosis increases genetic variability from one generation to the next, which matters for evolution. (v) False – in plant cells the wall formation starts in the centre as a cell plate and grows outward; a furrow is seen in animal cells. Four statements are correct.
